The teacher uses pictures or mimes to elicit some activities, e.g.: swim, cook, ride a bicycle, sing, climb a mountain …… etc.
The teacher shows the learners a picture of a boy with a tablet and asks the following questions:

T shows his pps a tablet and writes some questions on the board:
- Who has a tablet at home?
- What **can** we do with tablets?
- **Can** you write an email in Arabic?
- **Can** you write an email in English?
- **Can** you write an email in Chinese?
- Why?

**T highlights the rules:**
! To talk about things I or another person can do, I use: **can + verb** (ability).
! Example: I **can write** an email in Arabic.
! To talk about things I or another person can’t do, I use: **can’t + verb** (inability).
! Example: I **can’t write** an email in Chinese.
! To ask questions about ability / inability, I use: **Can + subject + verb**
! Example: Can you play the guitar?
! Yes, I can.
! No, I can’t.

T highlights the different ways to pronounce ‘can’. Example:
- Can you swim? /kən/
- Yes, I can. /kæn/
- No, I can’t. /kɑːnt/

(‘Can’ is weak in ‘Can you swim?’ because it isn’t stressed. It is strong in ‘Yes, I can’ and ‘No, I can’t’.)
PPs drill chorally and individually the different pronunciations of can and can’t.
The teacher devotes time to show the learners the difference between the sounds /ə/, /æ/ and /ɑː/ by doing task A page 17.

rows: Game: T invites his learners to move in the class and find who is fond of nature: birdwatching, flowers, plants, whale watching, picnics ……….
Brainstorm ideas about interests and pave the way

T invites his learners to work in small groups or in pairs to read the following short text and fill in the gaps with: flowers – goes – loves – books – places
> My brother Hamid …………. hiking. He always …………. for a long walk to discover new …………… but my sister Samira is fond of botany. She sometimes reads …………….. about plants and …………. at weekends.

T asks his learners to classify the missing words (flowers – goes – loves – books – places) according to the pronunciation of their final “s”.
|/s/|/z/|/ɪz/|
|---|---|---|
| | | |

T presents the rules from My pronunciation tools page 18.
! ‘s’ is pronounced /s/ in words that end in the following consonant sounds: /f/, /k/, /p/, /t/, /θ/.
! ‘s’ is pronounced /z/ in words that end in the following vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u) or consonant sounds: /b/, /d/, /g/, /l/, /m/, /n/, /r/, /v/.
! ‘s’ is pronounced /ɪz/ in words that end in the sounds: /tʃ/, /s/, /dʒ/, /z/, /ʃ/ – plurals and verbs that end in: -ches, -ces, -ges, -ses, -shes, -sses, -xes, -zes.

To encourage the Ls to work in groups or in pairs

To introduce the different sounds of the final “s”

To present the rules related to the pronunciation of the ending “s”

T invites his pps to listen and tick the right pronunciation of the final “s” (**task 7 page 20**).
The teacher invites his learners to read again My pronunciation tools 2 and correct each other.
T invites his learners to do **task 9 page 20**: they listen and match each word with the corresponding pronunciation of its final “s”.

T invites his learners to work in pairs and ask each other the following questions, then transform the information into a short piece of writing.

rows:
Teacher greets his learners and shows them a picture of a famous retired sportsman, e.g. Maradona, Belloumi or any other sportsman, then asks some questions:
- Who is this?
- What did he use to be?
- Does he still play …?
To pave the way for the presentation

T asks his pps to work in small groups, read the following dialogue and put it in the correct order (number one is done):
> **Journalist:** What sports **did** you **use** to do when you were a child?
> **Karim:** I **used to play** it every day.
> **Journalist:** When **did** you **use** to play football?
> **Karim:** I **used to play** football.
> **Journalist:** Do you play football now?
> **Karim:** No, I don’t.

The teacher invites his learners to read the dialogue and sort out sentences which talk about something that happened in the past.
The supposed answer:
- ==I used to play football.==
- ==I used to play it every day.==

The teacher devotes time to present the rules focusing on the right pronunciation of **used to** /juːstə/.
! T tells his pps that they can use the semi-modal verb **used + verb** to talk about repeated actions or activities which happened in the past but are no longer true in the present.
! Example: **I used to play football.**

The teacher presents the rule (the form and the meaning):
! 1) **Interrogative form:**
! Did you use to help your mother?
! Did + S + use + to + verb + the rest of the sentence
! 2) **Negative answer:**
! a) Short answer: No, I didn’t.
! b) Long answer: No, I didn’t use to help her.
! 3) **Affirmative answer:**
! a) Short form: Yes, I did.
! b) Long form: Yes, I used to help her.

To introduce the target structure in context

Highlighting rules

To familiarize the learners with the target structure focusing on the right pronunciation

T invites his learners to work in pairs and check the answers of each other and correct them.

**Note: the teacher should devote time to highlight rules:**
! To talk about the material (plastic, glass, iron, silk, wool, cotton, gold, wood …… etc.) something is formed of, I use: “**made + of + the name of the material**”.
! Example: Bottles are usually made of plastic or glass.
! To ask about material I can say: **What is it made of?**
! To talk about the place (city, country …) where an item is manufactured (produced / made), I use: “**made + in + the name of the place**”.
! Example: This jacket is made in France.
! To ask about the place where something is made I can say: **Where is it made?**
! To talk about food ingredients I use **made with** instead of **made of**.
! **Example:** The soup is **made with** vegetables and chicken.
